demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Vikram had spent forty years reading the water, but the storm that turned his life sideways had come through the coastal pines. He had been securing the winch line on the cutter when the wind shifted. He remembers the slickness of the coil, the sudden jerk of the metal, and then the sound that cut through the squall. When the fog cleared in his mind, there was only the shape of Officer Delaney crumpled near the railing, the bright crimson spreading across the gray deck, and the frantic barking of the medical team over the radio. He had been responsible for the line. He had been the one who read the tension wrong. The memories never settled into a clean sequence. They arrived as sharp, disconnected fragments: the smell of wet canvas, the vibration of the winch handle in his palms, the distant wail of the ambulance siren climbing over the water. He could not pull them together. When he tried to force them into order, his mind went blank, leaving only a hollow ache behind his ribs. He had come to believe the event was a fluke, that it had not been that bad, that the ocean had simply taken what it wanted. He built a careful architecture of positive thoughts around the silence where the memory lived, forcing his mind toward sunlit mornings, steady tides, and decades of quiet service. He pushed the rest out, day after hour. The quiet certainty that there was something wrong with him as a person arrived on the same deck and never left. He was certain that the accident was the proof of his character. He had always known he was the sort of man who let things go wrong. The hypervigilance settled in his shoulders like a second uniform. He scanned every room for exits, for weight-bearing surfaces, for any sign of instability. He stopped driving to unfamiliar towns. The roads shifted, the landmarks disappeared, and he could not assess the danger if the emergency happened again. Alongside the avoidance, he took risks he never would have in uniform—speeding down the coastal highway at dusk, leaning out to check a fishing line from the end of a dock, testing his balance on wet rocks. He always claimed the chair closest to the door in the veterans’ hall, the one backed by a solid wall, because only there did he feel protected. The consequences accumulated quietly. His daughter stopped inviting him to family dinners because he refused to go to restaurants in new neighborhoods. The assistant chief position ended when the department required inspections in ports he no longer recognized. He transferred to the records desk without protest. His wife, before the illness took her, had learned to speak only in the present tense. What frightened him most was the word future. When someone mentioned what might happen next, his throat closed. The talk of tomorrow felt like a tripwire, echoing the sudden, irreversible shift that had severed his life into before and after. He avoided planning for his own care, deflecting every question with a practiced smile or a sudden silence. At eighty, widowed and living alone in the same coastal cottage, Vikram finally recognized that the architecture was no longer holding. The recent diagnosis from his cardiologist, the sudden urgency in her voice about what his next steps should be, had left him unable to sleep. He drove himself to the community health center on the day the siren from a nearby fire drill echoed off the water. He sat in the waiting room, back to the wall, clutching a paper cup until his knuckles whitened. When he walked along the marsh trails near his house, the familiar pines and brackish water triggered a sudden, suffocating awareness of the exact place where his hands had failed. The memory would return not as a recollection but as an invasion. Every sense flooded at once: the bite of the salt wind, the metallic taste of adrenaline, the crack of the winch, the heavy silence that followed. He stood perfectly still until the wave passed. He was not there for his heart. He was there because the fragments were no longer staying buried, and he wanted to know if a man could finally step off the deck of his own making.
